We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on a particular type of manifold, which has properties similar to those of round spheres. Our findings show that this deformation theory can be equivalent to the deformation theory of Killing spinors, which are influenced by a particular vector field. When the manifold has a certain characteristic, its instantons can be mapped one-to-one to these spinors, and the deformation process can be directly related to the action of a specific linear transformation. This connection allows us to determine the deformation process's stabilizer and establish that for certain manifolds, the deformation process has no solutions unless a specific condition, related to the vector field, is satisfied. Our findings also show that when the manifold has a certain characteristic, the deformation process can be expressed as the union of round spheres, and any given instanton can be uniquely deformed to a manifold with a distinct G2 structure. Our results can be extended to more complex manifolds containing singularities and provide examples of manifolds with a G2 structure for which the deformation process has multiple solutions and is non-trivial.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition established by C. Pearcy, involving the operator's polar decomposition. Specifically, $T$ is C-normal if and only if there exist operators $T_1$ and $T_2$ such that $T_1$ is quasi-nilpotent, $T_2$ is normal and positive, and $TT_2 = T_1^*T_1$. The present paper expands upon prior research by showing that a restricted class of C-normal operators, namely those with compact resolvents, can be precisely defined by a straightforward condition involving their numerical radius.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic collection of significant p-core p'-partitions that establish a substantial new lower limit on their maximum size.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 26.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We introduce a simulation environment to examine slot allocation, specifically clear channel assessment, and its effects on network efficiency via simulated two-dimensional radar layouts in both ordered and random configurations. Our analysis compares the performance of four algorithms: Random Back-Off, Fitter, Fitter-Improved, and CCHF. Notably, CCHF has previously shown positive results in specialized scenarios; however, this study extends its application to various FMCW radar configurations. Interestingly, CCHF consistently demonstrates superior performance across different configuration settings, except when slot allocation is perfectly synchronized. To enhance fairness, we suggest modifying CCHF to prioritize older transmissions.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. A supporting model portrays the sample as an energy-preserving spectral filter, aligning with the observed results and providing insight into the entangled two-photon absorption process. By combining cutting-edge quantum interference techniques with a detailed mathematical framework, this work presents an innovative perspective on ETPA research.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graphs that incorporate time-specific information are crucial for accurately encoding real-world phenomena. Recent developments in deep learning have led to the adoption of sequential neural networks for processing time-sensitive data, such as language and biological sequences. In contrast, the design of deep neural architectures for temporal knowledge graphs remains largely rooted in static graph models. This work introduces Temporal Neural Relevance Model, a generative model that uses a sequential RNN to model TKGs. Experiments on various TKG benchmarks have shown TNM's performance to be on par with or surpassing state-of-the-art methods, with a significant improvement in handling time-sensitive relationships.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at a shallow angle relative to the listener's location.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research focus. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This advancement introduces a novel concept known as sufficiency, which enables the identification of suitable elements for "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. By incorporating sufficiency, it becomes possible to identify a more expansive group of elements compared to what was thought possible. This greater flexibility in element selection is demonstrated through the application of our findings to a specific scenario involving the CHSHine phenomenon.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in chiral systems with an imbalance in sublattices fall into this category. Following a general description of constructing flat bands through MOs, various examples are examined with numerical proof, including the sawtooth hypercube model and a sublattice version of the Berthier-Kosterlitz model.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the efficacy of electron-phonon interaction. Further analysis into potential improvements reveals that doping this system with electrons or holes yields unsatisfactory results. Ultimately, the critical temperature's limitations stem from the vanishing hydrogen influence on the Fermi level states, predominantly controlled by boron's p states.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve, with a specific sequence, denoted by $f_n$, initially presented in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences with the label A124324. This paper identifies a revised formula for calculating the $f_n$ value and uses this formula to find a relationship between the sequence and a specific type of division, referred to as the $e_n$ value. Additionally, the study explores the sequence in relation to another type of division, illustrated through an example involving the number 8.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable in length.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this capacity, prompting us to propose an advanced method centered around formal verification, leveraging model checking in particular. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we carefully recreate the driving system's dynamics, define and formalize key safety criteria, and scope the analysis within the guidelines specified by ISO 26262. Upon successfully verifying a high-automation fail-safe logic aligned with industrial standards, we discovered critical errors previously unaccounted for in more conventional evaluations, thereby enhancing the reliability of fail-operational systems and shielding against potentially hazardous system states.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a union of nested dynamical states. This framework is initially applied to simulated data and then tested on real-world datasets, yielding promising results in the identification of clusters in an air pollution network and a biomedical gene expression study.

Recent studies on Leibnizian calculus claim various achievements, but few provide clear directions on how to properly interpret Leibnizian calculus within modern mathematical frameworks. Evaluating these studies requires a thorough examination of the underlying metaphysics and mathematics attributed to Leibniz, particularly in relation to the fundamental concept of infinitesimal. This paper undertakes a comprehensive analysis of four prominent approaches to Leibnizian calculus and finds that only the non-standard analysis framework accurately represents Leibniz's metaphysics and calculus, with key affirmations including the reality of infinitesimal and continuum, as well as the independence of metaphysics from mathematics. Additionally, this paper challenges the prevalent myth that Leibniz's metaphysics was influenced by his mathematics or vice versa.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted, comparing these to actual data from real surveys like EDGES, FORNAX, and GASS. The impact of incorporating a non-zero neutrino mass and run-by-run non-Gaussianities into the analysis is also examined, along with how restricting certain parameters might improve the overall precision achieved. The ultimate precision that we can hope to achieve is discussed in relation to what is considered fine structure in cosmological data analysis.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their explicitly rated items. Various hybrid methods integrating document modeling and collaborative filtering have not been thoroughly explored. This research fills this knowledge gap by proposing the Document-Augmented Hybrid Deep Model (DAHD) that utilizes deep learning and incorporates both methods. By aggregating the strengths of mainstream deep recommender systems and hybrid models, DAHD achieves state-of-the-art performance in real-world datasets.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the emergence of expected conditional freeness in weak order $N^{-1}$ for all rotationally invariant random matrices. We've also identified novel relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and rotationally invariant freeness.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that the primary source of isospin breaking arises from transition matrix $T$ terms exhibiting isospin breaking and that additional isospin breaking arises due to the presence of loops containing kaons, as these do not cancel out when charged and neutral kaon masses differ. A calculated branching ratio for $a_0(980)$ production was found to be on the order of $5 \times 10^{-6}$. It is suggested that forthcoming experiments be conducted to investigate this problem, with the ultimate goal of better understanding scalar resonances through measurements of the $\pi^0 \eta$ mass distribution.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, while b) a field tracker captures images of the science target; c) a pupil imager re-images the telescope's pupil, and d) an aberration tracker captures images of a Shack-Hartmann sensor. The camera's detector images are analyzed using dedicated software to determine beam stabilization parameters, every 0.7 seconds. The resulting parameters are then applied to a) adjust the GRAVITY instrument to align with VLTI; b) actively stabilize the telescope's pupil and field of view; c) perform defocus correction, as well as various engineering tasks. The camera has successfully transitioned into operational use, with data reduction and on-sky characterization results having been documented.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with a limited set of supplier doubling dimension values and a specified number of anomalies. Conversely, for the more constrained Capacitated $k$-Center issue - a subset of CkSwO, - we demonstrate that achieving an analogous parameterized solution when dealing with highway dimension is computationally challenging, falling under the W[1] hardness class, whereas we find it relatively simpler with doubling dimension values.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper follows up on [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17] by refining those results in two key ways: introducing a new evaluation bound with reduced dependence on errors and an improved algorithm that requires fewer evaluations than previous methods, with a focus on small error rates; both results aim to close the gap between proven bounds and achievable solutions.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2^n correlations, maintaining even parity. Notably, this emission pattern can be perfect at specific driving frequencies "tuned to Tonks regime frequencies" and is resilient to dissipation effects. The stability of this emission pattern in the face of dissipation gives rise to a distinct cooling limit, transitioning from Lamb shift induced decay to a decay determined by the Rabi frequency and parity-protected emissions.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in the presence of chiral imbalance are explored by incorporating a local $U_A(1)$ symmetry into the linear sigma-model. The model's effective Lagrangian is developed to include vector mesons, assuming a broken $U_A(1)$ symmetry with a specific action and local $U_A(1)$ symmetry with a different action. By minimizing the quadratic effective actions for the vector mesons, mass spectra are calculated and the decay widths for the vector mesons decaying into electron-positron pairs are determined. The influence of chiral imbalance on the vector mesons' masses is found to vary significantly.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a node's distance to the majority of other nodes in a network that is attacked by malicious entities attempting to deceive us. Research has explored various methods for addressing this problem, but a crucial gap in knowledge remains to be filled. In this work, we develop a reliable distance estimation algorithm to a central node under attack by malicious entities, assuming only a limited number of malicious entities are present. Our algorithm is based on a model where the attack is initiated, has a certain duration, and can be stopped. Furthermore, we establish a network where a central node seeks to estimate its distance to a majority of other nodes in a network attacked by malicious entities. Our algorithm is grounded in statistical principles and is based on estimating a node's distance to the majority of other nodes in a network attacked by malicious entities. Assuming certain conditions are met, we can determine the number of malicious entities and provide an accurate estimate of the distance to a majority of other nodes. Our algorithm is tolerant of up to three malicious entities and achieves an accurate estimate of the distance to a majority of other nodes. Our algorithm also achieves an accurate estimate of the number of malicious entities and provides an accurate estimate of the distance to a majority of other nodes. Our algorithm is based on an analysis of a system's eigenvalues and is grounded in a reliable estimation algorithm that can determine a node's distance to a majority of other nodes in a network attacked by malicious entities. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Our proposed method is illustrated using an example with a scalar field, and we demonstrate that initially specified perturbations, such as scalar field perturbations, are preserved throughout the time evolution.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment depends on a precise energy scale in relation to an extensive energy reference, provided by an external neutron source. However, various factors within the experiment's early energy range cause uncertainties in this reference scale. Therefore, a study was conducted to assess the impact of these uncertainties on JUNO's ability to determine the neutrino mass ordering.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of LSTF, involving the prediction of multiple time steps ahead in a sequence, poses significant model demands, such as capture of long-term trends and dynamic interactions. The recent emergence of transformer models has addressed some of these challenges, but they often struggle with long-range forecasting due to high model parameter constraints. The Novel Deep Self-Attention for Long Sequences (DASAL) was developed to enhance the long sequence capacity of transformers through the incorporation of novel deep self-attention module. The DASAL module is characterized by four layers of self-attention that utilize adaptive gate units for parameter efficiency, accompanied by deep features for extended observation intervals. The results have shown that DASAL outperforms the current state-of-the-art approaches on LSTF tasks by a significant margin of 26.6%.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range, but can actually be searching for much larger and unexplored ranges of frequencies. A network of sensors, by cross-correlating their measurements, can detect these low-frequency fluctuations, and is not limited by bandwidth because low-frequency fluctuations will occur simultaneously at a range of frequencies. In this way, existing sensor networks can be used to experimentally explore the unexplored ranges of the parameter space of this bosonic dark matter.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The weight of each Dirac mass is determined through the computation of a particular least-squares problem involving the original Fourier coefficients and the assumed low-frequency Fourier coefficients.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison.

In numerical simulations, the transport equation for vector fields is commonly used in fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics. To efficiently solve this equation, we have developed a high-order semi-Lagrangian method. This approach involves using a higher-degree polynomial for the function space, which allows for more accurate representations of the vector fields, resulting in lower errors compared to lower-degree polynomials. By testing the method, we have found that it outperforms existing methods, such as finite element and Lagrangian methods, in various settings. For example, when we used the method to simulate a simple circulation in a square domain, we achieved low errors of $0.02$ or smaller for the $L^2$-norm. We have also demonstrated the method's applicability in more complex simulations by modeling a vortex ring in a finite domain and a turbulent flow in a square domain with random initial conditions.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental testing of this solution on the popular WMDS dataset demonstrated superior results, outperforming the individual applications of each method alone.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian systems led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general problems with constraints.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a sophisticated update method for neural network training that leverages specialized networks to efficiently refine parameters in large, pre-trained models. By segmenting the network into manageable "layers," our method applies separate critic networks to each layer, updating parameters within each segment while keeping others fixed during training. Critic networks are critical to our training procedure, as they enable the optimization of parameters without the need for gradient descent on the entire model. We have found that our training procedure not only accelerates training but also significantly reduces the memory requirements typically associated with generating gradients for large models. We have thoroughly tested our method and have seen substantial improvements in both efficiency and performance in tasks such as image classification and language modeling. Our results demonstrate that local critic training is a versatile and practical technique for training large-scale neural networks, especially those based on transformer architectures.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such circumstances. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research highlights the potential for Wada basins to survive dissipation and suggests that Wada basins can persist in higher-dimensional systems as well.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes of these scalar particles at beam dump experiments, such as the Drell-Yan process, heavy meson decay, and muon scattering, to derive constraints from the CHARM and NuTeV experiments and gauge the detection capabilities of the upcoming SHiP beam dump experiment which has the ability to exhaustively explore the mass window linked to the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
interpretable and reliable performance, even when trained entirely on publicly
available VOC07 and UCF101 datasets with strong difficulty levels. Key strengths 
of HAN include its ability to effectively capture complex temporal structures 
in high-level actions through the integration of bottom-layer features and the 
dynamic exploration of temporal information through the incorporation of 
input-dependent temporal weights. Furthermore, HAN's separate path for 
downsampling features enables the focus to be centered on prominent objects, 
enabling the extraction of meaningful action features. Through extensive testing 
on challenging action classification benchmarks, HAN has achieved outstanding 
performance, with particular notable success on TUD-Cross-Segment and Trento 
datasets where generalization to unseen classes is evaluated.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such a process. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black hole mass and charge is not satisfied is that the singularity remains hidden.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planets have been discovered everywhere in the sky. Fresh data from multiple sources, including wide-field telescopes like the VLA, CARMA, and ALMA, are incorporated to inform the article. 

As the universe evolved, the first stars, rich in heavy elements, formed in large molecular clouds, triggering the formation of the first planets. The symbiotic relationship between stars and planets persisted, with the former influencing the latter's development and characteristics. Lately, stars have been forming at a slower rate due to interactions with other stars, the interstellar medium, and possibly other factors, leading to a decline in their movement and mass in the past 100 million years. 

In the local galaxy, stars form in dense, molecular clouds, and their movement and mass are influenced by the clouds' movement and mass, revealing a new understanding of the relationship between stars and the interstellar medium. This perspective offers a comprehensive view of the star formation process, and its relationship with planets, from the beginning to the present day.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state when transportation costs are involved. Novel contributions to addressing this issue include deriving a necessary condition for a converging sequence of solutions and proving the existence of a globally convergent algorithm for certain structured problems. Furthermore, we provide an illustrative example to demonstrate the applicability of our findings in a particular setting that has eluded solution for over a decade.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The deployment of these classifiers on IoT devices, which often lack processing power or have limited memory, becomes impractical, leading to a major limitation. The integration of green technology, specifically renewable energy sources, into cybersecurity, although relatively new, has immense potential to overcome these limitations, as demonstrated by our case study incorporating photo voltaic energy into IoT-based cybersecurity.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We then explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a Krull dimension of k, it will have a Schreier growth gap of n^k, such as the Schreier growth gap n^d for the wreath product C_p ∋¬ ℤ^d and n^(d+1) for ℤ ∋¬ ℤ^d. For solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank, a Schreier growth gap of exp(n) applies unless they are virtually nilpotent, a criterion which also applies to solvable groups linear over ℚ. Lastly, a wide range of torsion-free solvable groups have a Schreier growth gap of n^2, a group type that also includes those linear over ℚ.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset comprising a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the development of more effective detection methods.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations through their inverse measurements. While this paradigm promises a new way of scientific inquiry, it's unclear whether it's truly compatible with the long-established and validated principles of physics. Attempts to use ML for this purpose have yielded mixed results, with a few notable successes in simplified systems but mostly negative outcomes in more complex real-world scenarios. By reflecting on the fundamental properties of matter and energy, as described by the theory of relativity and quantum mechanics, we examine whether the inverse measurement approach can be consistent with these established physics rules. We highlight the challenges that arise when trying to derive universal physical laws through machine learning, specifically difficulties in handling multiple possible solutions, addressing phase transitions, and accommodating non-trivial relationships between objects and their properties. Therefore, we believe that ML, AI, and traditional physics cannot coexist in a way that prioritizes one over the other without conflicts and incompatibilities. Nevertheless, we propose that the exploration of the inverse measurement problem can serve the physics community as a tool to reinforce and validate long-established theories, rather than replace them.

This study explores the discovery potential of massive, long-lived, charged particles in the ATLAS detector at the LHC, focusing on particles created through beyond-the-standard-model processes. To enhance detection efficiency, the analysis combines large tracking data sets from collisions at 13 TeV and high-luminosity runs at 14 TeV. To account for the uncertainty in the luminosity during data collection, two methods are employed: one uses a reference cross-section and estimates the uncertainty statistically, while the other uses a benchmark cross-section and a simulation-based analysis. To identify these particles, three key characteristics are targeted: a distinct track lasting the lifetime of the particle, high transverse momentum, and an unusual energy distribution along the track. To minimize background from standard-model processes, a multivariate classifier is developed using machine learning techniques. To validate the methodology, the sensitivity is assessed for the production of two LHC supersymmetric top types: a color-octet pair and a gluino-squark pair. However, this study shows that the ATLAS detector has the capability to exceed the sensitivity of other experiments for the production of these massive, long-lived, charged particles.

We have developed a numerical method to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by optimizing a 2D cross-section. Using the vectorial mode expansion method, we calculated the mode overlap between the quantum dot and the fundamental mode of the ridge waveguide, weighing the effects of mode mismatch and green light exclusion in GaAs platforms. Iterative optimizations have indicated that a large Purcell factor can be achieved with a relatively narrow gap between the quantum dot and the light source. However, this setup may cause mode loss in the GaAs platform, leading us to develop an optimization technique to balance Purcell factor and light confinement factors. As a result, we obtained a 79.8% efficient design with a high Purcell factor of 45.9% and a significant improvement in light efficiency, offering a viable pathway to rapid development of reliable single-photon sources.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' reach, making numerical simulation methods 
like MADGRAPH 5.a the standard approach. However, this leaves a gap in 
understanding fundamental physics for its own sake. We propose a new, 
semi-analytical method building on recent technical breakthroughs to bridge 
the gap between precision physics and fundamental understanding.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at about 15-20 km per second. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable widths and features including distinct, inward-pointing spiral patterns. Based on further examination using 21-cm data, it's found that these patterns extend as far as 2-3 milliparsecs in radius and that the distance between the arms is uniform at about 0.7 milliparsecs. Both arms appear to originate from a circular pattern at a radius of approximately 0.25 milliparsecs and share similar characteristics in their emission intensities. This similarity in structure and pattern suggests that the Galaxy's central 200 light-years exhibits a radial symmetry, which is consistent with theory suggesting that the spiral pattern in the Galaxy's central region is approaching a stable structure resembling those found in external galaxies.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate applications of these optimization techniques.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach is NP-complete, even when using limited binary valuations. However, under the condition of binary and symmetric valuations, we found that a stable matching will always exist and can be found within polynomial time. Additionally, we looked at finding the best stable matches that maximise total happiness when using binary and symmetric valuations. While finding the absolute optimum is a complex problem, we identified a more practical solution for approximating it closely.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. Valley Hall response
is found to be largely unaffected by static strain but highly sensitive to dynamic
mechanisms, where the type of convolution (as opposed to the usual product) plays a
key role. This discovery broadens the scope for utilizing valley Hall effect in
solid-state devices, suggesting the possibility of tuning the valley Hall signal
using strain modulation rather than destroying it.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. Our work identifies a set of'symptoms' that flag whether a space belongs to this class, and we prove that the closure of any cloud of spaces contains a unique subspace, also a cloud, with a simpler structure.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the first two resonances and a microstrip matching circuit that optimally adjusts the resonant frequencies, lengths, and distances between the microstrip feed and the patch. The presented antenna exhibits an excellent agreement between the simulated and measured performance, with a maximum peak gain of about 5.9 dBi, a low sidelobe level of about 3.2 dB, and a wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to ultimately develop a training strategy aimed at enhancing the code's error correction capabilities. Through this approach, the results illustrate a considerable boost in performance, as evidenced by the successful extension of surface code sizes and also the successful implementation of efficient real-time decoding in cases involving constant, recurring errors.

Quantum metrology enhances precision in measurements by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and has been discovered to provide equal precision to more complex approaches, despite only relying on single particles and simple feedback circuits for its implementation.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased production, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions at large angles. This indicates an abundance of low-momentum-colorless particles in $d$$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Fragments from hot accretion disks, which could supply these particles, are a potential explanation for these observations.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the connection topology of qubits, our results indicate that a specific arrangement - a chain with every other qubit connected - is the most efficient for simulating Fermi-Hubbard. Furthermore, our corrections were able to restore accuracy under realistic conditions where qubit connectivity was imperfect, confirming the value of digital-analog methodology in the exploration of novel many-body systems.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, thereby limiting their potential. This work explores an alternative approach, which involves using rich, well-structured initialization for neural networks. Our method draws on the concept of expert initialization, where individual layer parameters are uniformly distributed across a comprehensive set. This innovative technique offers several advantages. Firstly, it facilitates streamlined hyperparameter tuning, as its parameters are inherently robust and easy to replicate. Moreover, rich initializations tend to converge to more stable, generalizable models, even when trained over a wider range of epochs. Furthermore, they demonstrate a significant generalization improvement when compared to their counterpart – the Adam initializer.

To further augment the performance of rich initializations, we introduce two additional modules: Batch Estimation Module (BEM) and Direction Estimation Module (DEM). Which one is chosen is determined by a new module, the Which Estimation Module (WEM), also based on BE and DE. These modules are designed to analyze batch and iteration statistics, providing more accurate model initialization and thereby enhancing optimization and generalization. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of our initialization method, along with the added modules, in domestic and zero-shot semantic segmentation scenarios.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm designed to locate the optimal positioning of micro-LEDs for efficient light focusing within a scattering medium. In our proposed solution, a weight matrix is introduced to prioritize search efficiency by constraining the movement of individual LEDs within their respective emission properties, and a mutant operator based on noise adaptation ensures robust search results. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm, we used both numerical and experimental approaches to investigate and confirm its ability to find the optimal LED arrangement for efficient focusing of 630nm light through a 2cm thick scattering medium with varying levels of scattering density. In comparison to alternative optimization methods, our proposed algorithm consistently yields higher energy densities and more precise beam similarity.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem, demonstrating that existing methods cannot satisfy both retargeting and efficient evaluation constraints under certain conditions. In contrast, we propose a new retargeting approach for efficient policy evaluation that meets both constraints, thus offering a more general and efficient solution. In Section 3, inspired by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we design a retargeting procedure for efficient policy evaluation, meeting both requirements. Furthermore, when data from the testing distribution is available during training, our research shows that retargeting and efficient policy evaluation constraints can be efficiently satisfied. In Section 4, through simulations and real-world studies, we validate the efficiency of our proposed retargeting procedure for efficient policy evaluation.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth for small collection electrodes through numerical simulations, focusing on a prototype sensor designed for the ATLAS detector's future upgrades. The simulations examine the charge collection dynamics and hit detection efficiency in response to fluences relevant to upcoming experiments, revealing improved performance with high-resistivity Czochralski substrates compared to standard epitaxial materials. The results indicate a high detection efficiency even when the sensor depth exceeds 300 micrometers, offering sufficient lifespan for sensors exposed to lower levels of radiation before reaching end-of-life.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of thousands of frames per second even in the presence of extremely rapid changes in the atmosphere. We have tested the effectiveness of the FAST system in a laboratory setting, simulating the kind of fast movements the atmosphere can exhibit, and found that it outperforms other similar systems by successfully reducing the speckle noise and allowing the differentiation of objects with differences of under one tenth of a pixel.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations are performed, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations, to showcase the benefits of this model, as evidenced by its similarity to the Hull-White one-factor model's Bermudan swaption prices on Bloomberg, while also successfully addressing the negative interest rate issue.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past predictions made for LBNE. We visualize these results for each neutrino type – electron, muon, and tau – indicating that DUNE has a promising capacity to explore previously unexplored areas of the parameter space before the SHiP experiment joins similar research initiatives.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix, resulting in asymptotic equivalence to previously proposed estimators such as the bias reduced linearization, while also providing improved bias in finite samples sizes.  Through Monte Carlo simulations it has been demonstrated that the new estimators outperform existing robust estimators in terms of accuracy in cases of small numbers of studies and also show improved performance in cases of normally distributed and non normally distributed effects.  The new estimators have been implemented in the package lansdron R package available on the CRAN.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially stretching time steps, but this can lead to inaccuracies in simulations by not properly accounting for collision impacts on turbulence and sediment transport. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes a novel method for resolving collisions, combining it with existing models to form a comprehensive framework. Simulation results indicate that even small changes in collision time steps have a significant effect on particle entrainment and flow turbulence. Therefore, accurate simulation of turbulent flows and sediment transport using traditional models requires extremely small time steps, making the method inefficient for large-scale simulations. Our integration algorithm effectively addresses this limitation, allowing simulations to be conducted with larger time steps while maintaining good agreement with detailed models. Additionally, we observe decreased error rates as time increments increase.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to yield transverse momentum variations consistent with measured values, especially in cases where rapidity is in the forward direction. Additionally, model consistency with ALICE measurements is found across various centrality levels.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it possible to achieve this, as data in non-volatile memory remains intact even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a significant challenge, as data in these caches is lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new method based on a color coding technique is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems employing non-volatile memory. This approach exploits the properties of non-volatile memory to build a reliable snapshot, which in turn enables the reconstruction of accurate and consistent data in the event of a crash. In a comprehensive evaluation, our method demonstrated superior crash recovery time and superior scalability compared to existing methods, with particular success in situations involving large data sets and slow data flush times. In addition to these findings, our method was found to be compatible with various data parallelism models at a conceptual level, as well as several system architectures that support fault tolerance.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds agreed well with an independent, flux-based prediction. Both findings support the flux-based three-body statistical framework, and our measurements of absorptivity and lifetime distributions provide valuable resources for further testing and validation of statistical models.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum levels above 25 GeV/$c$ when compared to lower momentum levels. The study found that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is greater than that of J/$\psi$ mesons over the entire examined momentum range.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine.
This hyperdoctrine can be embedded in a suitable category of topological spaces,
whose objects are defined by a topological space along with a choice of open
sets, and whose arrows are defined by continuous functions that preserve the
selected open sets.
The hyperdoctrine's fibers are equivalent to the logic's meaning for a fixed
language, and the hyperdoctrine's structure allows for the definition of
certain equivalence relations on predicates, which correspond to the notions of
algebraic equivalence and semantic equivalence in continuous logic.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states through the use of a position embedding scheme that draws parallels to Cosine Analysis. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate the capability of this method to forecast suicidal ideation with an error rate of 92.6%, a 4.6% improvement over the baseline which solely utilizes EHR data.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE.
